2. Detect cycles (A→B→C→A) and peel chains (descending amounts hop-by-hop) in the counterparty graph.

statutory.question: Does the conduct described fall within 5318(g)?
statutory.answer: Yes, 31 U.S.C. § 5318(g) requires reporting of these transactions because the activity is highly suspicious.
statutory.label: entailment
statutory.reasoning: Under 31 U.S.C. § 5318(g) requires reporting of transactions that have no apparent lawful purpose or are not the sort in which the particular customer would normally be expected to engage. The fact pattern shows Entity SYN_13f68eea, an offshore holding company with a declared monthly volume of $170,920, conducted six wire transfers totaling over $915,000 within a single week (April 11 to April 17, 2026). This volume vastly exceeds the expected monthly volume. Furthermore, every transaction is flagged as a 'peel-chain hop,' a technique typically used to obscure the origin and destination of funds. Because the activity is inconsistent with the entity's profile and exhibits hallmarks of money laundering, it triggers the reporting requirements of 31 U.S.C. § 5318(g).

sar_output.suspicious_activity_report: Entity SYN_13f68eea, a BVI-incorporated offshore holding company, exhibited a rapid-movement wire pattern consistent with a peel-chain. Between 2026-04-11 and 2026-04-17, the entity executed six wire transfers to distinct counterparties (including VXUFU Imports LLC and TICZ Logistics LLC) totaling $915,178.54. This activity represents a volume ratio of 26.77x the declared monthly volume of $170,920.00. The transactions show a descending amount pattern (peel-chain) inconsistent with the entity's declared purpose of asset holding. This conduct triggers reporting requirements under 31 U.S.C. § 5318(g) as it lacks an apparent lawful purpose and deviates from the customer's profile. Final filing decision is deferred to the human investigator.
